title: CELPIP General Listening — Practice Test 13
instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

parts.title: Problem Solving
parts.description: A conversation in which one person has a problem and seeks help from another.

parts.title: Daily Life Conversation
parts.description: An everyday conversation between two people.

parts.title: Listening for Information
parts.description: An informational talk; listen for specific details.

parts.title: Discussion
parts.description: A discussion among people with different viewpoints.

parts.title: Viewpoints
parts.description: A longer talk presenting one speaker's opinion and reasons.

listeningScripts.title: A Repair Quote That Doubled
listeningScripts.text: Caller: I'm calling about the invoice for my boiler. The quote was three hundred and eighty and the bill is seven hundred and ten. Office: Let me pull the job up. Was that the Kingsway Road address? Caller: That's right. Tuesday last week. Office: I have it. The engineer's notes say the pump was replaced as well as the valve. Caller: I know. He told me. But he told me while he was doing it, not before. Nobody asked me whether I wanted a pump at that price. Office: That's fair, and it isn't how it is meant to go. Our engineers are supposed to stop and call the office for anything that takes a job more than twenty per cent over the quote. Caller: This is nearly double. Office: It is. Here is what I can do. I can put the invoice on hold while I speak to the engineer, and that stops any late payment charge building up while we sort it out. What I can't do is tell you today what the outcome will be, because I need his side of it. Caller: How long? Office: He's on a job in Carlisle until Thursday. I'd say Friday for an answer. Caller: And if he says he did ask me? Office: Then it goes to my manager, and at that point the question is whether there is a written record. There isn't one on our side. He didn't log a call to the office, and that is the part I would say doesn't help him. Caller: The pump did need replacing, I'll say that much. It's the price I object to, not the work. Office: Understood, and that is worth saying to the manager. It is a narrower argument than asking for the whole thing back, and narrower arguments tend to do better.

listeningScripts.title: A Shared Fence After the Storm
listeningScripts.text: A: Have you had a look at the fence since the storm? B: The panel by the shed. I saw it this morning. A: Two panels, actually. The one by the shed is leaning, and the next one along is off its post entirely. B: Right. So is that yours or mine? I've never actually known. A: Nor have I. The deeds say the boundary is ours to maintain, but the fence was already there when we bought the house, so I don't know that those are the same thing. B: My view is we split it and don't look it up. Whatever the paperwork says, we would both rather have a fence than be right. A: Agreed. Do you want to get a quote, or shall I? B: You get one, I'll get one, and we go with whichever is lower. That way neither of us is choosing our brother-in-law. A: Fair enough. One thing. I'd like the new panels a bit lower than the old ones. The old ones take the light off my kitchen in the afternoon. B: Lower is fine by me, as long as the dog can't see through it. He barks at everything that moves. A: Solid panels, just shorter. That works for both of us. B: When are you free for them to come round? I'm away until the twelfth. A: Then let's say the weekend after.

listeningScripts.title: New Tenant Building Orientation
listeningScripts.text: Welcome to the building. I'll take about ten minutes, and everything I say is in the tenant handbook as well — that's the green one. The blue one is the fire plan, and you should read that one too. Laundry is in the basement, and it runs on the app rather than on coins. Machines can be booked up to two days ahead, in two-hour slots. If you don't turn up within fifteen minutes of your slot starting, the machine releases and anyone can take it. That fifteen minutes is not negotiable, because we went through a period where people booked every evening for a month and used about half of them. Bins. The chute on each floor is for household waste only. Recycling goes to the bays behind the building, and I want to be precise about this, because it is where we get charged. Cardboard has to be flattened. If it isn't, the city treats the whole bay as contaminated and bills the building, and that bill goes into next year's fees for everybody. Parking. Each unit has one space. Visitor parking is the eight spaces nearest the road, three hours maximum, with a permit from the app on the dashboard. There is no overnight visitor parking at all, and cars are towed rather than ticketed, so please do tell people. The buzzer connects to your phone rather than to a handset in the flat. If you change your number, you have to tell the office, or your buzzer will ring a number that isn't yours. Repairs. Anything that is flooding, sparking, or has left you without heat goes to the emergency line, which is answered at any hour. Everything else goes through the app, and the target is three working days. If you report a dripping tap at two in the morning on the emergency line, it will still be logged as routine, and you will have woken somebody up for nothing.

listeningScripts.title: Nunavut Community Freezer Programme Expands
listeningScripts.text: The territorial government will expand its community freezer programme to eleven more hamlets over the next two years, more than doubling the number taking part. Community freezers hold country food — caribou, char and seal — donated by hunters, so that anyone in the hamlet can take what they need. The nine existing freezers distributed about forty thousand kilograms last year. The expansion will cost three point four million dollars. About a third of that is not the freezers themselves but the electricity and the maintenance, which have been the difficulty in the past: two of the original freezers stood empty for a year because the hamlet could not meet the running costs. Hunters' organisations welcomed the announcement but asked for a fuel subsidy alongside it, arguing that a freezer is only useful if somebody can afford to get out on the land in the first place. The department said fuel sits outside this programme, but is being looked at separately. The first four new freezers are due to be installed before freeze-up next autumn.

listeningScripts.title: Dropping the Attendance Requirement
listeningScripts.text: Okafor: The proposal is to drop the ten per cent attendance mark from first-year courses, and let the grade rest on the work. Arsenault: Then half my nine o'clock stops coming, and the ones who stop coming are the ones who most need to be there. I can see it in the marks. Students who miss the first three weeks don't recover. Menon: They don't recover, no. But is that because they missed the class, or because whatever made them miss the class is still going on? Most of the students I hear from are not skipping. They are working a shift, or they have a child, or the bus from the east end doesn't get here in time for a nine o'clock. Arsenault: All true, and none of it changes what the marks do. Okafor: The mark punishes the same students twice, though. If you are working a shift, you lose the class, and then you lose the ten per cent for having lost the class. Arsenault: Then let me record the lectures, and count watching one as attendance. Menon: That I would support. But a recorded lecture without the seminar is not the same course, and the seminar is where the work actually happens. Arsenault: Then let attendance count for seminars and not for lectures. That is the half of it I actually care about. Okafor: Seminars only, at five per cent rather than ten? Menon: Five I could defend to students. Ten reads as a threat. Arsenault: I would want it reviewed after a year, with the first-year pass rate set beside it. Okafor: That's reasonable. I'll draft it that way.

listeningScripts.title: Replacing Tipping With Higher Prices
listeningScripts.text: Every few years a restaurant announces that it is abolishing tipping, raising its menu prices and paying a proper wage. And then, eighteen months later, a fair number of them quietly go back. I want to work out why, because the reasons are not the ones people usually give. The obvious explanation is that customers hate the higher prices. There is something in it, but less than you would think. What the research shows is that customers compare the menu price, not the total. A twenty-two dollar dish beside a competitor's eighteen looks worse, even though the eighteen becomes twenty-two once the tip is added. The comparison happens before the bill arrives, and by the time the bill arrives the choice has been made. The bigger problem is inside the restaurant. Servers at busy, expensive places often earn more on tips than any flat wage a restaurant can offer them, so the best of them leave. Meanwhile the kitchen, which is the whole reason for going, has been on a flat wage all along and gets no share of the tips at all. That gap between the front of house and the back is the thing abolition is genuinely trying to fix, and the gap is real. But abolishing tips fixes it by making the front worse off, which is exactly why the front leaves. So what actually works? The places that made it stick did two things. They did not do it alone — they did it in a city where enough restaurants moved at once that the menu price comparison stopped biting. And they raised kitchen pay first and visibly, so the staff who lost tip income could see what the money had bought. My honest position is this. The practice is bad, the arguments for ending it are sound, and a single restaurant ending it on its own will usually fail for reasons that have nothing to do with whether it was right.

questions.prompt: Why is the caller telephoning?
options: The bill is far larger than the quote
The boiler has failed again since the repair
The engineer did not arrive on the agreed day
An invoice has arrived for work at another address
questions.correctAnswer: The bill is far larger than the quote
questions.explanation: The caller opens with the figures: a quote of three hundred and eighty against a bill of seven hundred and ten.

questions.prompt: What extra work was carried out?
options: A valve was replaced twice
The boiler was replaced entirely
A pump was replaced as well as a valve
A second engineer attended the job
questions.correctAnswer: A pump was replaced as well as a valve
questions.explanation: The engineer's notes record the pump being replaced in addition to the valve, which the caller does not dispute.

questions.prompt: What is the caller's actual objection?
options: The extra work was not necessary
The engineer never mentioned the extra work at all
The invoice arrived later than promised
He was told about the extra work only while it was being done
questions.correctAnswer: He was told about the extra work only while it was being done
questions.explanation: The caller says the engineer told him during the work rather than before it, so nobody asked whether he wanted a pump at that price. He accepts later that the pump did need replacing.

questions.prompt: What are engineers supposed to do in this situation?
options: Obtain a signature from the customer on site
Telephone the office before going more than twenty per cent over the quote
Finish the job and flag the cost on the invoice
Issue a fresh written quote before continuing
questions.correctAnswer: Telephone the office before going more than twenty per cent over the quote
questions.explanation: The office says engineers must stop and call the office for anything taking a job more than twenty per cent over quote — and this job is nearly double.

questions.prompt: What does putting the invoice on hold achieve?
options: It prevents late payment charges building up
It cancels the disputed part of the bill
It passes the case straight to the manager
It guarantees a decision within five days
questions.correctAnswer: It prevents late payment charges building up
questions.explanation: The office can hold the invoice so no late payment charge accrues during the dispute, while being clear that the outcome itself is not decided by that.

questions.prompt: Why can there be no answer before Friday?
options: The manager is away until the end of the week
The invoice cannot be reviewed until it is overdue
The engineer's notes have not been filed yet
The engineer is working in Carlisle until Thursday
questions.correctAnswer: The engineer is working in Carlisle until Thursday
questions.explanation: The engineer is on a job in Carlisle until Thursday, so the office expects to have his account by Friday.

questions.prompt: What does the office say weakens the engineer's position?
options: He has had complaints of this kind before
He made no logged call to the office
His notes contradict the invoice
He did not obtain a signature
questions.correctAnswer: He made no logged call to the office
questions.explanation: There is no written record on the company's side, because the engineer did not log a call to the office — the part the office says does not help him.

questions.prompt: What does the office advise the caller to argue?
options: That the whole invoice should be cancelled
That the pump did not need replacing
That the price is wrong rather than the work
That the engineer should attend a second time
questions.correctAnswer: That the price is wrong rather than the work
questions.explanation: The office points out that objecting to the price while accepting the work is a narrower argument than asking for the whole thing back, and that narrower arguments tend to do better.

questions.prompt: What damage has the storm done?
options: One panel, leaning against the shed
The posts along the whole boundary
Two panels and the shed roof
Two panels, one leaning and one off its post
questions.correctAnswer: Two panels, one leaning and one off its post
questions.explanation: A corrects B: it is two panels rather than one — the one by the shed is leaning and the next along is off its post entirely.

questions.prompt: What do the deeds say?
options: The boundary is B's to maintain
The boundary is A's to maintain
The fence is jointly owned
The deeds do not mention the boundary
questions.correctAnswer: The boundary is A's to maintain
questions.explanation: A says the deeds put the boundary on their side, while doubting that this settles who owns a fence that was already standing when they bought the house.

questions.prompt: What do they decide about the cost?
options: To split it without checking who is responsible
To ask A's insurer to cover it
To split it once the deeds are checked
For A to pay, as the deeds indicate
questions.correctAnswer: To split it without checking who is responsible
questions.explanation: B proposes splitting it and not looking it up, on the grounds that they would both rather have a fence than be proved right, and A agrees.

questions.prompt: Why will they each get a quote?
options: Because the insurer requires two quotes
So the work can start sooner
So that neither of them chooses a relative
Because they disagree about the design
questions.correctAnswer: So that neither of them chooses a relative
questions.explanation: B suggests one quote each and taking the lower, so that neither ends up choosing their brother-in-law.

questions.prompt: What do they agree the new fence should be like?
options: Solid panels, but lower than the old ones
The same height, in a lighter material
Lower panels with gaps between the boards
Whatever the cheaper quote recommends
questions.correctAnswer: Solid panels, but lower than the old ones
questions.explanation: A wants lower panels for the kitchen light; B agrees provided the dog cannot see through, so they settle on solid panels that are simply shorter.

questions.prompt: Which handbook contains the fire plan?
options: The green one
The blue one
Both of them
The one in the laundry room
questions.correctAnswer: The blue one
questions.explanation: The green handbook covers what the talk itself covers; the blue one is the fire plan, which the speaker says should also be read.

questions.prompt: What happens fifteen minutes after a laundry slot begins?
options: The booking is charged to the tenant anyway
The slot is extended automatically
The tenant loses booking rights for a month
The machine is released for anyone to take
questions.correctAnswer: The machine is released for anyone to take
questions.explanation: A machine not claimed within fifteen minutes releases to anyone, a rule the speaker calls non-negotiable after a period of people booking slots they did not use.

questions.prompt: Why must cardboard be flattened?
options: Flattened cardboard is collected more often
The bays are too small otherwise
The city charges the building for a contaminated bay
The chute cannot take unflattened boxes
questions.correctAnswer: The city charges the building for a contaminated bay
questions.explanation: Unflattened cardboard makes the city treat the whole bay as contaminated and bill the building, with the bill landing in next year's fees for every tenant.

questions.prompt: What is the rule for visitor parking?
options: Three hours at most, with none overnight
Three hours at most, extendable through the app
One space per unit, overnight permitted
Eight hours at most in the spaces nearest the road
questions.correctAnswer: Three hours at most, with none overnight
questions.explanation: Visitors may use the eight spaces nearest the road for three hours with an app permit, and there is no overnight visitor parking at all — offenders are towed rather than ticketed.

questions.prompt: What belongs on the emergency line?
options: Anything reported outside office hours
Flooding, sparking, or a loss of heat
Any repair not fixed within three working days
A dripping tap, if it cannot wait
questions.correctAnswer: Flooding, sparking, or a loss of heat
questions.explanation: The emergency line is for flooding, sparking or no heat. A dripping tap reported at two in the morning is still logged as routine, so the call achieves nothing but waking someone.

questions.prompt: What must a tenant do after changing their phone number?
options: Reconnect the handset in the flat
Update the app within three working days
Nothing, because the app updates itself
Tell the office, or the buzzer will ring the wrong number
questions.correctAnswer: Tell the office, or the buzzer will ring the wrong number
questions.explanation: The buzzer rings the tenant's phone rather than a handset, so an unreported number change leaves the buzzer ringing somebody else.

questions.prompt: What is being expanded?
options: A community freezer programme, to eleven more hamlets
A hunting licence scheme, to eleven more hamlets
A food shipping subsidy, to nine more hamlets
A freezer repair programme across the territory
questions.correctAnswer: A community freezer programme, to eleven more hamlets
questions.explanation: The programme goes to eleven more hamlets over two years, more than doubling the nine already taking part.

questions.prompt: What do the freezers hold?
options: Food bought in bulk by the hamlet
Emergency supplies held for the winter
Country food donated by hunters
Food shipped in from the south
questions.correctAnswer: Country food donated by hunters
questions.explanation: The freezers hold country food — caribou, char and seal — donated by hunters, available to anyone in the hamlet.

questions.prompt: What has caused difficulty in the past?
options: A shortage of donated food
The cost of electricity and maintenance
The distance between hamlets
Freezers breaking down in summer
questions.correctAnswer: The cost of electricity and maintenance
questions.explanation: About a third of the cost is running the freezers rather than buying them, and two of the original nine stood empty for a year because the hamlet could not meet those costs.

questions.prompt: What did hunters' organisations ask for?
options: A larger number of freezers
Payment for the food they donate
A say in where the freezers are placed
A subsidy for fuel
questions.correctAnswer: A subsidy for fuel
questions.explanation: They welcomed the announcement but asked for a fuel subsidy too, arguing a freezer is only useful if somebody can afford to get out on the land.

questions.prompt: How did the department respond to that request?
options: Fuel will be added to the programme next year
The request was refused outright
Fuel falls outside this programme but is being considered separately
Hamlets may use the maintenance budget for fuel
questions.correctAnswer: Fuel falls outside this programme but is being considered separately
questions.explanation: The department said fuel sits outside this programme but is being looked at separately — neither a refusal nor an inclusion.

questions.prompt: What does Okafor propose at the start?
options: Reducing the attendance mark to five per cent
Applying the attendance mark to seminars only
Removing the attendance mark from first-year courses
Recording lectures so students can watch them later
questions.correctAnswer: Removing the attendance mark from first-year courses
questions.explanation: The opening proposal is to drop the ten per cent attendance mark altogether and let the grade rest on the work. The five per cent and the seminars-only limit are where the discussion ends up, not where it starts.

questions.prompt: What evidence does Arsenault give?
options: Students who miss the first three weeks do not recover
Attendance in her nine o'clock has already halved
Students say they prefer compulsory attendance
Pass rates fell the last time the rule changed
questions.correctAnswer: Students who miss the first three weeks do not recover
questions.explanation: Arsenault says she can see it in the marks: students who miss the first three weeks do not recover. The halved nine o'clock is what she predicts, not what has happened.

questions.prompt: What is Menon's answer to that?
options: The marks are measured in the wrong way
Three weeks is too short a period to judge
Attendance has no effect on results at all
The cause of the absence may be what prevents recovery
questions.correctAnswer: The cause of the absence may be what prevents recovery
questions.explanation: Menon accepts that they do not recover but asks whether that is the absence itself or the shift work, childcare or bus timetable that is still going on. He does not dispute the figures.

questions.prompt: Why does Okafor say the mark punishes students twice?
options: Late work is penalised as well as absence
A student who loses a class also loses the marks attached to it
The mark counts in every first-year course
Students who miss seminars also miss the lecture
questions.correctAnswer: A student who loses a class also loses the marks attached to it
questions.explanation: Okafor's point is that a student working a shift loses the class and then loses the ten per cent for having lost it.

questions.prompt: What does Arsenault suggest first?
options: Moving the nine o'clock class to a later hour
Excusing students who are in paid work
Recording lectures and counting a viewing as attendance
Raising the attendance mark above ten per cent
questions.correctAnswer: Recording lectures and counting a viewing as attendance
questions.explanation: Arsenault's first suggestion is to record the lectures and count watching one as attendance, which Menon says he would support in itself.

questions.prompt: Why is Menon uneasy about that suggestion?
options: Recordings would reduce lecture attendance further
Watching a lecture leaves out the seminar, where the work is done
Not every student can watch a recording at home
Recording lectures is too expensive to do
questions.correctAnswer: Watching a lecture leaves out the seminar, where the work is done
questions.explanation: Menon would support the recordings but says a recorded lecture without the seminar is not the same course, because the seminar is where the work happens.

questions.prompt: What do the three of them settle on?
options: Attendance counted for lectures only, at five per cent
Dropping the mark for a year as a trial
Keeping the ten per cent but only for seminars
Attendance counted for seminars only, at five per cent
questions.correctAnswer: Attendance counted for seminars only, at five per cent
questions.explanation: Okafor proposes seminars only at five per cent rather than ten; Menon says five is defensible to students where ten reads as a threat, and Arsenault accepts.

questions.prompt: What does Arsenault ask to be added?
options: A review after a year, alongside the pass rate
A vote of the first-year students
An exemption for students in paid work
A record of which seminars each student attends
questions.correctAnswer: A review after a year, alongside the pass rate
questions.explanation: Arsenault's condition is that the change be reviewed after a year with the first-year pass rate set beside it, and Okafor agrees to draft it that way.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say happens about eighteen months later?
options: Menu prices are raised a second time
Other restaurants copy the change
Customers stop noticing the difference
A fair number of restaurants return to tipping
questions.correctAnswer: A fair number of restaurants return to tipping
questions.explanation: The pattern the talk sets out to explain is that a fair number of the restaurants that abolish tipping quietly go back about eighteen months later.

questions.prompt: Why do higher menu prices cause trouble?
options: Customers cannot afford the higher prices
Menu prices rise by more than the tip was worth
Customers compare the menu price rather than the final total
Customers assume the food has changed
questions.correctAnswer: Customers compare the menu price rather than the final total
questions.explanation: The research says customers compare menu prices: twenty-two beside a competitor's eighteen looks worse, even though the eighteen becomes twenty-two once the tip is added, and the comparison happens before the bill arrives.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say happens to servers where tipping is abolished?
options: The best of them leave, because tips beat any flat wage
Kitchen staff resent the change
Customers tip on top of the higher prices anyway
Restaurants cannot calculate the new wage correctly
questions.correctAnswer: The best of them leave, because tips beat any flat wage
questions.explanation: The speaker puts this inside the restaurant rather than in front of the customer: servers at busy, expensive places earn more on tips than a flat wage can match, so the best of them leave for somewhere that still pays them.

questions.prompt: Which gap is abolition genuinely trying to close?
options: The gap between expensive and cheap restaurants
The gap between the front of house and the kitchen
The gap between menu prices and the final bill
The gap between busy and quiet nights
questions.correctAnswer: The gap between the front of house and the kitchen
questions.explanation: The kitchen has always been on a flat wage and shares in no tips, and the speaker calls the front-to-back gap the real thing abolition addresses — while noting that abolition closes it by making the front worse off.

questions.prompt: Besides raising kitchen pay first, what did the places that made it stick do?
options: They raised prices gradually over two years
They kept tipping for the kitchen only
They were less expensive than their competitors
Enough restaurants in the same city moved at once
questions.correctAnswer: Enough restaurants in the same city moved at once
questions.explanation: They did not do it alone: enough restaurants in the city moved at the same time that the menu price comparison stopped biting, and they raised kitchen pay first and visibly.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker's own position?
options: Tipping should be left alone until customers change
The case for ending tipping is sound, but one restaurant alone will usually fail
Ending tipping works wherever kitchen pay rises first
The evidence is too mixed to take a position
questions.correctAnswer: The case for ending tipping is sound, but one restaurant alone will usually fail
questions.explanation: The speaker holds that the practice is bad and the arguments against it sound, while a single restaurant acting alone usually fails for reasons unconnected to whether it was right.
